extracted.intended_audience: systematic reviewers, meta-analysts, health technology assessment researchers, and health researchers evaluating dissemination/publication bias
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical criteria for detecting and handling different types of dissemination/publication bias (outcome reporting, time lag, grey literature, language bias, selective analyses) when conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses in health research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome reporting bias (compare protocols vs publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary outcomes specified in protocols may differ from primary outcomes stated in subsequent journal articles; many outcomes listed in protocols are incompletely or not reported in publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare trial protocols with publications to identify discrepancies. The review reports primary outcome changes in 62% (Danish cohort) and 40% (Canadian cohort). Statistically significant outcomes are more likely to be fully reported (odds ratios reported: efficacy OR 2.4 and 2.7; harms OR 4.7 and 7.7). Expect lower response rates from trialists and possible underestimation of bias if relying on investigator surveys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective reporting of multiple alternative analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials may present multiple analyses for the same outcome (e.g. ITT vs per-protocol) but publications often report the more favourable analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check submitted reports/protocols for all analyses performed (e.g. ITT and per protocol). Be wary of stand-alone publications that report only the more favourable result. Where possible extract and report all analysis types or contact authors for unreported analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time lag bias (time to publication depends on result)
rubrics_metrics.description: The speed of publication can depend on the direction and strength of study results; significant/positive studies are often published earlier than non-significant ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure time to publication using an explicitly defined start point (REC approval, funding date, enrolment start/finish, completion of follow-up, or manuscript submission). Examine cohorts of studies for differences in median time-to-publication by result (examples: significant results published sooner; HRs and medians provided in multiple studies). Recognise that time lag bias likely occurs before manuscript submission rather than after.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in reported effect size over time ('fading' of reported effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported treatment effects may decrease over time as later trials are published; early trials can overestimate treatment effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate temporal trends of effect size within meta-analyses (cumulative/meta-regression by year). Case studies found early trials often reported larger effects; this can indicate time lag bias but is not the only possible explanation. Limited research exists; treat temporal trend evidence cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grey literature bias (inclusion/exclusion of grey literature affects estimates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Published literature tends to report more positive estimates of effectiveness than grey literature; grey literature encompasses non-commercially published material (conference abstracts, reports, theses, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider searching for and including grey literature, but apply quality assessment since grey studies can be smaller or poorer quality. Empirical studies found published trials on average suggest greater treatment effects (pooled RORs reported ~1.07–1.15 in cited studies). Make inclusion decisions case-by-case; inclusion may sometimes introduce bias and exclusion may also bias results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language bias (effects of excluding non-English studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences may exist between English and non-English language trials (size, methodological quality, likelihood of positive results), but non-English studies should not be excluded solely on language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include trials regardless of publication language when feasible. Empirical findings are mixed: some analyses show minor differences in quality, others show non-English trials smaller or more likely to report significant results. Do not generalise exclusion based on language; assess study quality individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of IPD versus published-data meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: IPD (individual patient data) meta-analyses may include more trials and can produce qualitatively different results compared with meta-analyses based only on published summary data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where outcomes are vulnerable to selective reporting (e.g. subjectively assessed outcomes like persisting pain), pursue IPD if possible, since it may retrieve additional trials and change conclusions (case: hernia recurrence vs persisting pain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess completeness/usability of reported results for meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all reported results are usable in meta-analysis (e.g. missing data, insufficient detail); a substantial proportion of reported results may be unusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and report the proportion of results usable for meta-analysis (example: Bekkering found 61% of reported results usable). Be aware that usable results were more likely to indicate the existence of associations than unusable ones — this can bias pooled estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess proportion of contributing RCTs to pooled estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Within a meta-analysis, only a subset of identified RCTs may contribute to pooled estimates due to incomplete reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the proportion of eligible RCTs that contributed data to pooled estimates (example: median 46% in Furukawa et al.). Examine relationship between proportion contributing and pooled effect size; smaller proportions may be associated with larger effects, suggesting bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contacting trialists for unreported data (practical consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreported data may sometimes be available from original investigators, but obtaining it can be time consuming and often unsuccessful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt contacting authors where key outcomes are missing, but plan for low response and potential resource burden. Document attempts and consider sensitivity analyses to explore the impact of missing/unobtained data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential under-reporting of harms versus efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm (adverse event) data are more likely to be incompletely reported than efficacy outcomes, and selective reporting of harms can be severe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give particular attention to harms reporting: compare protocols, regulatory data (e.g. CDUS/FDA) and publications. Be aware reported odds ratios indicate larger bias for harms (examples provided). Under-reporting of low-grade adverse events is common (example: only 58% of low-grade events reported in articles vs CDUS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analysis and imputation for missing outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When within-study outcome reporting bias is suspected, sensitivity analyses (including imputation of missing results) can assess the potential impact on pooled estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform sensitivity analyses with plausible imputations for missing outcomes to evaluate robustness (Williamson & Gamble example decreased pooled effect when imputing missing results). Report how conclusions change under these scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess quality of grey literature and potential bias from its inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Grey literature studies vary in quality; inclusion can both reduce and introduce bias depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same quality criteria to grey literature as to published studies. Examples show grey literature can be higher, lower, or similar quality; assess geographic and topic coverage advantages (e.g. operational research in grey literature) and weigh these in inclusion decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution when using conference abstracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Conference abstracts often provide limited information, may report partial datasets, and may be misleading compared with later full publications; many abstracts never reach full publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abstract data cautiously: note limited details and potential for change on full publication. Track subsequent full publications where possible and consider risk of selective full publication when including abstract data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly define start point when measuring time-to-publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Time to publication can be measured from many milestones (REC approval, funding received, initiation/completion of enrolment, completion of follow-up, manuscript submission), and choice affects results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and justify the chosen start point for time-to-publication analyses. Different start points may yield different conclusions about time lag bias; compare results across plausible definitions when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare published data with regulatory or other complete data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons between published trial reports and regulatory databases (e.g. FDA reviews, CDUS) or other fuller data sources can reveal selective publication and reporting distortions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where accessible, compare journal publications with regulatory data or clinical study reports (examples: Turner et al. FDA vs publications showed published articles had larger effect sizes and non-publication of negative trials). Use such comparisons to quantify likely bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document reasons for non-reporting and consider their implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors state reasons for not reporting outcomes (space constraints, lack of clinical importance, statistical non-significance), which affect interpretation of reporting bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and report stated reasons for non-reporting when available (examples: space constraints 47% for efficacy, lack of importance 37%, non-significance 24%). Consider how these motivations could systematically bias available evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine between-study variance/heterogeneity over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in between-study variance over time may indicate selective early publication of heterogeneous or contradictory results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse temporal trends in heterogeneity (Ioannidis & Trikalinos found early heterogeneity larger for genetic associations). Interpret changes alongside potential causes other than dissemination bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cumulative/meta-analytic approaches to evaluate the effect of including unpublished data
rubrics_metrics.description: Cumulative meta-analysis or adding unpublished/regulatory data can show whether inclusion changes effect estimates or interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply cumulative/meta-analytic methods to see if conclusions shift when unpublished or grey literature data are added (case examples where inclusion changed or did not change interpretation). Report these influence analyses to inform robustness.
